## Overview

The Tigray (*Tegaru*, sing. *Tegaray*) are a Semitic-speaking people of the northern Ethiopian highlands, inhabiting the Tigray Region of Ethiopia between the Tekezé River and the Eritrean frontier, with closely related communities — the Tigrinya (*Bihere Tigrinya*) — across the border in the Eritrean highlands, and diasporic populations in Addis Ababa, Khartoum, the Gulf, and across Europe and North America. Their language, *Tigrinya* (*Tigrigna*), belongs to the Ethiopic branch of South Semitic and descends, together with Ge'ez and Amharic, from the epigraphic South Arabian and Aksumite linguistic milieu; it is written in the *Fidäl* syllabary inherited from Ge'ez. Total Tigrinya-speaking population is commonly estimated at around 9–10 million, of whom roughly 7 million live in Ethiopia proper. The Tigray consider themselves the direct heirs of the Aksumite state (c. 1st–8th c. CE), whose monumental stelae, coinage, and adoption of Christianity in the 4th century under Ezana laid the substrate for highland Ethiopian civilisation; the ancient capital *Aksum* remains the ceremonial heart of the Ethiopian Orthodox *Täwaḥədo* Church and, in tradition, the resting place of the Ark of the Covenant (*Tabota Ṣəyon*). In folk-culture terms the Tigray matter as custodians of the Aksumite lithic and manuscript tradition: the granite obelisks and rock-hewn churches of Gheralta and Tembien, the *Ge'ez* illuminated gospels and *ma'ihafa* codices of the highland monasteries, the crossmaking of Aksum and Adwa, and the finely woven *netela* shawl of the highland woman.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Netela** (*ነጠላ*) — the sheer white handwoven cotton shawl worn draped over the shoulders and, in church, drawn up over the head. Woven on a pit treadle loom from hand-spun cotton (*ṭit*), it carries at one or both ends a coloured warp-and-weft border, the *tibeb* (ጥበብ, "wisdom" or "craft"), embroidered or supplementary-weft woven in geometric bands.

**Tibeb** — the decorative border itself, ranging from a narrow red-and-gold stripe to broad polychrome panels with stepped diamonds, cross motifs, and stylised church-window lattices. In Tigray the palette tends to be more restrained than in southern Amhara work, with heavier use of deep red, indigo, and metallic thread.

**Kuta / gabi** — the *kuta* is a thicker single-layer wrap for men, the *gabi* a heavy multi-layer cotton blanket-shawl worn against highland cold; both are woven in undyed cotton with minimal border decoration.

**Weaving organisation.** Cotton is spun by women on the drop spindle (*inzirti*) and traditionally woven by men, in many districts by members of endogamous artisan lineages sometimes referred to as *shimagle* weavers, though the caste-like stratification is less rigid than among some southern Ethiopian groups.

**Motif vocabulary.** Cross forms (*mesqel*) in stepped, lobed, and interlaced variants; the eight-pointed star (*kokäb*); the church-window lattice (*mesekot beta krestiyan*); rhombic amulet forms; and stylised palm and vine borders derived ultimately from late-antique Mediterranean and Coptic prototypes.

### Clothing & dress

Everyday men's dress in the countryside is a knee-length white cotton tunic (*qemis*) worn over jodhpur-cut trousers, wrapped with a *kuta* or *gabi* against the cold, with a shepherd's staff (*dula*) and, historically, a curved sickle-sword (*shotel*) or straight dagger. Women wear the long white *qemis* — cut wider and longer than the men's, often with an embroidered *tibeb* panel down the front placket, at the cuffs, and around the hem — cinched with a woven sash and covered by the *netela*. For high feasts and weddings the ensemble is a *habesha kemis*, a full-length white cotton gown with dense *tibeb* borders in coloured silk and metallic thread, worn with a matching *netela* drawn up over elaborately plaited hair. Married women in some rural districts still wear their hair in the *albaso* style — many fine braids close to the scalp gathered into a plaited crown — dressed with butter. Highland priests and *debtera* wear a white turban (*shash*), a white *netela*, and, in liturgical use, brocaded copes and embroidered vestments (*kaba*) modelled on Byzantine prototypes. Warrior dress, retained ceremonially, includes a lion's-mane headdress (*lämd*) and a rhinoceros- or hippopotamus-hide shield (*gasha*).

### Architecture

The signature Tigrayan built form is lithic and ecclesiastical. The Aksumite tradition, dating from the first millennium CE, produced the monumental granite *hawelti* (stelae) of Aksum — carved to imitate multi-storey timber-and-stone tower-houses, complete with false doors and beam-ends (*monkey-heads*), the tallest standing 24 m and the fallen Great Stele originally about 33 m — inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1980. The same Aksumite constructional grammar of alternating stone courses and projecting timber beam-ends survives in the vernacular *hidmo*, the flat-roofed, stone-walled, timber-beamed farmhouse of central and eastern Tigray, built of undressed basalt or sandstone laid dry or in mud mortar, with a beaten-earth roof over juniper joists and brushwood, entered through a low door and lit by narrow slit windows. The *hidmo* typically groups living quarters, grain store, and byre around or under one roof, on a stone plinth stepped into the hillside. In the western and southern lowlands the round thatched *agdo* or *tukul* — a conical grass roof on a wattle-and-daub cylinder — is more common. Ecclesiastical architecture ranges from the built basilicas of Debre Damo (a 6th-century monastery reached only by leather rope up a sheer cliff, one of the oldest standing churches in sub-Saharan Africa) through the rock-hewn churches of Gheralta, Tembien, and Atsbi — including Abreha we-Atsbeha, Wukro Cherqos, and the cliff-face sanctuaries of Maryam Korkor and Daniel Korkor — to modern circular churches with a central *maqdas* (sanctuary) housing the *tabot*. Interiors carry mural cycles in the Ethiopian Orthodox iconographic canon: wide-eyed frontal saints, equestrian warrior-saints, and Old Testament typologies.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Village pottery is hand-built (no wheel) and pit- or bonfire-fired by women potters, in some districts drawn from endogamous artisan lineages. Characteristic vessels include the tall-necked *jebena* coffee pot with a bulbous body and spouted lip, the wide-mouthed *ensera* water jar, the flat clay griddle (*mogogo*) on which *injera* is baked, and small incense burners. Metalwork is the province of male smiths (*tabib*), likewise historically endogamous and viewed with a mixture of respect and ritual wariness. Aksum, Adwa, and Adigrat are the historic centres of Ethiopian cross-making — hand processional crosses (*mäsqäl*) in brass, bronze, and silver, cast by lost-wax and finished by chasing and piercing, with the distinctive Tigrayan *Aksum cross* and *Adwa cross* subtypes characterised by dense interlace and radiating open tracery within a lobed outline. Neck crosses (*maţäb*) of the same design, worn on a blue-black silk cord from baptism, are the universal marker of Orthodox identity. Other metalwork includes the curved *shotel*, straight double-edged *seif* daggers with rhinoceros-horn hilts, and copper coffee trays. Domestic woodwork includes the low three-legged stool (*berchuma*), the round basketry table-hood (*mesob*) woven of dyed grass in concentric coloured bands, and carved wooden headrests.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Tigrayan personal ornament centres on silver and on the cross. The neck cross (*maţäb*) is worn from infancy; women often add a heavier pectoral cross (*mäsqäl*) on high feasts. Silver filigree and granulation, worked in Aksum and Adwa, produces earrings (*gwara*), forehead ornaments, and multi-strand chokers. Amulets in leather or silver cylinders (*kitab*) containing folded parchment prayers written by a *debtera* are worn against illness and the evil eye. Facial and neck tattooing — small crosses on the forehead, temples, chin, and gums, and lattice bands on the neck and hands — is traditional among Christian highland women, applied in childhood with soot and plant dye; the practice is receding but still visible among older women. Elaborate braided coiffures dressed with butter, sometimes with silver hair-pins, complete the ensemble. Bridegrooms are decked with a borrowed sword and shield; brides with a gauze *netela* embroidered in gold, silver anklets, and henna on the palms and soles in a practice shared with lowland Muslim neighbours.

## Music & performance

Tigrayan secular music is built around the five-string bowl lyre *krar*, the larger ten-string *begena* (the "harp of David", used devotionally), the one-string spike fiddle *masinko*, the end-blown flute *washint*, and the double-headed goblet drum *kebero*. Sung poetry favours the wax-and-gold (*säm-enna-wärq*) tradition of double meaning shared with Amharic, and the *melke'e* praise-poem genre. Wedding and threshing songs are typically call-and-response, led by a soloist (*azmari*) improvising verses on the guests, with the crowd answering a fixed refrain. The distinctive female ululation, *elelta*, punctuates every ceremonial climax. Liturgical music is the *zema* chant of the Ethiopian Orthodox *Täwaḥədo* Church, codified in tradition by the sixth-century Saint Yared into three modes — *ge'ez*, *ezel*, and *araray* — notated by *mələkət* neume-marks above the Ge'ez text and performed by *debtera* clerks who accompany themselves on the *kebero* drum, the *sanasel* sistrum (a direct descendant of the pharaonic instrument), and the prayer staff (*mäqwamiya*), on which they lean and beat time. The full liturgy of Aksum's Church of Maryam Ṣəyon on Hidar Ṣəyon is one of the great annual displays of this repertoire.

## Dance & theatre

The signature Tigrayan dance is *awris* (in some districts *quda* or *shushaye*), a shoulder dance in which men and women, standing in a loose circle or facing lines, isolate and pulse the shoulders rhythmically to *kebero* and clapping while the head and hips remain almost still — a movement vocabulary distinct from the more looping *eskista* of Amhara neighbours, though outsiders often collapse the two under the *eskista* label. Sword and shield dances (*shilela*) survive as martial display at weddings and at the *Ashenda* festival, with men leaping and boasting (*fukera*) their lineage and past deeds. There is no indigenous secular theatre tradition in the European sense; liturgical drama is embodied instead in the great processional *timkat* (Epiphany) and *mesqel* observances, and in the *debtera*'s sistrum-and-staff *aquaquam* — a slow, hieratic swaying dance performed in ranks before the sanctuary on major feasts, which functions as sacred performance.

## Festivals & rituals

The Tigrayan year is calibrated to the Ethiopian Orthodox calendar. *Mesqel* (Meskel, 27 September), commemorating the Finding of the True Cross by Empress Helena, is celebrated by lighting a great conical bonfire (*demera*) of daisy-covered poles in every village square — the practice is inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity (2013). *Timkat* (Ṭəmqät, 19 January) commemorates the Baptism of Christ; the *tabot* of each church is carried in procession under a canopy to a body of water, where the congregation renews baptismal vows at dawn — also inscribed by UNESCO (2019). *Hidar Ṣəyon* (30 November) is the great pilgrimage feast of Aksum, drawing tens of thousands to the Church of Maryam Ṣəyon. *Ashenda* is the distinctively Tigrayan girls' festival of mid-August, at the end of the *Filseta* fast, in which unmarried girls dress in new *habesha kemis* and beaded *ashenda* grass skirts and move from house to house singing, drumming on the *kebero*, and receiving small gifts; it is a rare public arena for female performance and courtship display. Fasting (*ṣom*) — no animal products on Wednesdays, Fridays, and through the long Lent (*Hudade*), Advent (*Ṣom Nabiyat*), and Filseta — structures the culinary year. Rites of passage include the fortieth-day (boys) and eightieth-day (girls) baptism, marriage by *qurban* church communion or by civil *serat* contract, and the *tezkar* memorial meal at the fortieth day, six months, and anniversary of a death.

## Foodways

The staple is *injera* — a large, spongy sourdough flatbread of fermented *ṭeff* (*Eragrostis tef*) batter, poured onto the hot clay *mogogo* and baked with a lid — served as both plate and utensil, with stews (*wat*) spooned on top and torn off with the right hand. *Ṭeff* is the highland grain par excellence and northern Tigray is one of its heartlands. Signature dishes include *shiro* (spiced chickpea or bean-flour purée), *misir wat* (red-lentil stew), *doro wat* (long-simmered chicken and boiled egg in *berbere* chilli sauce, the feast-day dish), *tsebhi sga* (beef stew), and *zigni* (a Tigrayan hot beef stew often distinguished from Amhara *wat* by a lighter hand with butter and a heavier one with chilli). *Berbere* — a paste of chilli, garlic, ginger, ajwain, korarima, long pepper, and fenugreek — and *niter kibbeh* — spiced clarified butter — are the two foundations of the sauce repertoire. Distinctively Tigrayan is *tihlo*, a stiff dumpling of roasted barley flour eaten with a fork-like wooden pick dipped into a communal *wat*, and *hilbet*, a raw legume-flour purée eaten during fasts. Coffee (*bunna*) — the plant is native to the Ethiopian highlands — is prepared in the *jebena buna* ceremony, roasted on the spot over charcoal, ground in a mortar, brewed in the *jebena* pot, and served in three successive rounds (*abol*, *tona*, *baraka*) over an incense burner, with popcorn or roasted barley (*qolo*). The Ethiopian coffee ceremony is one of the most tenacious rituals of daily hospitality. Local drinks include the honey wine *mes* (*tej*), barley beer *sowa* (*tella*), and, on fast-days, a barley infusion.

## Oral tradition & literature

Tigray sits at the origin point of the written literature of the Horn of Africa. *Ge'ez* — the classical Ethiopic language, no longer a mother tongue but preserved as the liturgical language of the *Täwaḥədo* Church — is written in the *Fidäl* syllabary, a descendant of the Sabaic South Arabian script, and provided the vehicle for the earliest Aksumite royal inscriptions (Ezana's trilingual, 4th c.) and for a vast subsequent manuscript literature: the Bible (with the distinctive Ethiopian Old Testament canon including *Enoch* and *Jubilees*), the national epic *Kebra Nagast* ("Glory of the Kings", 14th c.), which recounts the descent of the Solomonic dynasty from the union of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba (*Makeda*), the *Synaxarion* (*Senkessar*) lives of saints, and hymnaries (*Deggwa*) of Saint Yared. Manuscripts are copied on parchment (*bra'na*) prepared from goat or sheepskin, written with reed pen (*bǝr'e*) and lamp-black or vegetable ink, bound between wooden boards in tooled leather, and illuminated in the "First" and "Second" Gondarine styles inherited by Tigrayan monastic scriptoria at Debre Damo, Debre Abbay, and Waldibba. Vernacular Tigrinya oral genres include the *massé* praise poem, the *melke'e* portrait poem, riddles (*enqoqilesh*), proverbs (*mesalé*), and the wax-and-gold double-meaning verse shared with Amharic literary culture. A modern Tigrinya print literature emerged in the twentieth century, initially from Eritrean presses.

## Language & religion

*Tigrinya* is spoken by roughly 9–10 million people across Tigray and highland Eritrea and functions as the working language of the Tigray Region. Ethnic Tigrayans are overwhelmingly adherents of Ethiopian Orthodox *Täwaḥədo* Christianity, one of the Oriental Orthodox (non-Chalcedonian) communions, which has been the state church of the northern Ethiopian polities since Ezana's conversion in the 4th century. The church is organised around parish churches (each housing a consecrated *tabot* replica of the Ark), a strong monastic tradition of cliff and rock-hewn foundations, and the lay-clerical order of *debtera* who serve as chanters, scribes, and healers. A minority of Tigrayans — the *Jeberti* — are Sunni Muslims, historically merchants and long integrated into highland Tigrayan society, and there is a small Roman Catholic community around Adigrat dating from 19th-century missions. The Beta Israel (Ethiopian Jews) of the wider northern region, most now in Israel, shared many cultural forms with their Christian Tigrayan and Amhara neighbours. Pre-Christian and para-Christian practices persist in the veneration of the *zar* possession spirits, in the amuletic use of *kitab* scrolls prepared by *debtera*, and in the sacred groves and holy springs (*ṣäbäl*) attached to many church sites.
